fields.h1: The Master’s Indwelling by Andrew Murray: Summary and Study Guide
fields.meta_title: The Master’s Indwelling by Andrew Murray — Summary & Study Guide
fields.description: A reader’s summary and study guide to Andrew Murray’s The Master’s Indwelling: the carnal vs. spiritual Christian, the self-life, and the indwelling life of Christ — with themes, reading tips, and reflection questions. Read the full book free on Ochorus.
fields.body_html:
What the book is, and what Murray set out to do

If you have ever wondered why the Christian life so often feels like striving rather than rest, The Master’s Indwelling was written for you. In this short book Andrew Murray gathers a series of addresses he gave at the Northfield conference on one great theme: that the secret of a holy, restful, fruitful life is not more effort but a Person — Christ himself, dwelling within the believer by his Spirit. Murray’s aim is pastoral and searching. He wants to show the earnest but defeated Christian why the flesh keeps winning, and then to lead that same reader, step by step, out of self and into the indwelling life of the Master. Ochorus hosts the complete text free, and this guide is a map through it.

Murray begins where the Apostle Paul begins, with an uncomfortable diagnosis. Writing to the Corinthians, Paul distinguishes two kinds of believer — the spiritual and the carnal — and says he cannot feed the second the deeper things of God (1 Corinthians 3:1-3). That contrast between the carnal Christian and the spiritual Christian is the hinge of the whole book. Murray is not addressing the unconverted. He is addressing genuine believers who remain, in Paul’s words, babes in Christ (1 Corinthians 3:1), and he refuses to let that condition pass as normal.

Some have lived many years as believers, and yet always remain infants; others are spiritual men because they have given themselves up to the power, the leading, and the entire rule of the Holy Ghost.

Andrew Murray

How the book is organized

The Master’s Indwelling moves like a good sermon series: it wounds before it heals, and it does not hurry. Read in order, the chapters trace a single journey from the carnal life into the indwelling of Christ.

It opens with the carnal Christian — the believer who is truly in Christ yet governed by self, marked by envy and strife (1 Corinthians 3:1-3), living below what God intends. From there Murray turns to the root of the problem, the self-life, which he treats as the hidden spring of all our defeat. The middle chapters open the way into the spiritual life: waiting on God, entering into rest, seeking first the kingdom (Matthew 6:33), and the complete surrender of everything to Christ. Then come the chapters on the indwelling Christ himself — Christ our life (Colossians 3:4), Christ’s humility as our salvation, and the death to self by which we are joined to his risen life (Romans 6:11). The book closes on the work of the Spirit: joy in the Holy Ghost, the triumph of faith, the source of power in prayer, and the final aim that God may be all in all.

The order matters. Murray will not talk about the indwelling Christ until he has made you feel the poverty of the self-life, and he will not talk about power in prayer until you have learned to wait.

The central themes

The two lives: self and Christ

Beneath every chapter lies one great either/or. Murray insists that the reason so many Christians never grow is not weak effort but an unbroken self-life — and that self cannot be improved, only surrendered. He states the choice with startling plainness.

There are two lives, the self-life, and the Christ-life; I must choose one of the two.

Andrew Murray

This is why Murray dwells on death before he dwells on life. To be joined to the risen Christ is to reckon oneself dead to sin (Romans 6:11), for the believer’s life is now hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3). Only the soul that gives up the self-life is free to receive the Christ-life.

Murray is careful here in a way that spares the reader a great deal of frustration. The self-life, he argues, is not conquered by fighting it directly, as though holiness were a matter of self-discipline turned up higher. Self cannot cast out self. It is displaced only when a greater Presence moves in. That is why the book keeps returning from our striving to Christ’s indwelling: the point is never to become strong enough to defeat the flesh, but to become empty enough that Christ may fill and rule. The whole burden of 1 Corinthians 3:1-3 is that the carnal Christian is trying, and failing, to live a life only the Spirit can produce.

The indwelling Christ, by the Spirit

The title tells you where the book is going. Murray does not present Christ merely as an example outside us or a Saviour in heaven, but as a living Presence within, who wishes to live his own life through us. The one who makes this real is the Holy Spirit, and Murray is emphatic that no amount of resolve can substitute for the Spirit’s indwelling.

It is the Holy Spirit alone who by His indwelling can make a spiritual man.

Andrew Murray

Here the book breathes the same air as Paul’s great confession that it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me (Galatians 2:20), and as Jesus’ own picture of the branch that can do nothing apart from the vine (John 15:5). The fruit of that indwelling — love, joy, peace — is the Spirit’s own harvest (Galatians 5:22), not the product of our striving.

Waiting, rest, and surrender

Because the life is Christ’s and not ours, the believer’s first work is not activity but waiting. Murray returns again and again to the quiet posture of the soul before God, echoing the Psalmist’s resolve to wait in silence for God alone (Psalm 62:1).

Waiting on God is the first and the best beginning for prayer.

Andrew Murray

Out of waiting comes rest — the true Sabbath of the soul that ceases from its own works, which Murray frames through the summons to strive to enter that rest (Hebrews 4:11). And rest, in turn, is only entered through surrender. The condition Murray names, over and over, is a complete giving-up of self, so that Christ may reign. His counsel is not gentle, because he believes the stakes are joy itself.

Will you not choose a life in which God shall be all, and in which you rest in Him for all?

Andrew Murray

Humility as the doorway

True to the author of Humility, Murray makes lowliness the gate through which the indwelling life is entered. Christ’s own humility — the mind that emptied itself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:5) — is not only our example but our salvation, because it restores the creature to its right place of dependence on God. Self-exaltation and the Spirit’s fullness cannot share one heart.

This is one of Murray’s most freeing insights. Many readers arrive at a book like this expecting to be told to work harder at being good. Murray tells them almost the opposite: that the way up is down, and that the soul which consents to be nothing gives God room to be everything. Humility, in his hands, is not gloom about oneself but glad relief — the end of the exhausting project of managing our own righteousness, and the beginning of resting in Another. The believer who stops defending self is the one most quickly filled.

Who should read it

The Master’s Indwelling is for the Christian who is doing everything right and still feels dry. If you have been converted for years, know your Bible, keep the disciplines, and yet find that impatience, pride, and defeat keep resurfacing, Murray is speaking directly to your condition — the carnal believer of 1 Corinthians 3:1-3 who has never learned to yield to the indwelling Christ.

It is also for the reader hungry for the deeper life but wary of hype. Murray offers no technique and no dramatic second experience to chase; he offers a Person to surrender to. Pastors and small-group leaders will find in its short chapters a ready framework for teaching sanctification without slogans. And anyone who has loved Murray’s other books — Holy in Christ or The True Vine — will recognize the same warm, unhurried voice here, applied to the single theme of Christ within.

One caution: this is a convicting book. Murray means to unsettle the comfortable before he consoles the weary. Come to it willing to be searched.

How to read it today

Read it slowly, one chapter at a time, and let each one do its work before moving on. These began as spoken addresses, so they reward being read almost devotionally — a chapter a day rather than a book in a sitting.

  • Start with the diagnosis. Sit with the opening chapters on the carnal Christian and the self-life until you can honestly locate yourself. Murray’s whole cure depends on an honest diagnosis (1 Corinthians 3:1-3).
  • Keep a Bible open. Murray preaches straight from the text. Read his key passages for yourself — Romans 6:11, Colossians 3:3, Galatians 2:20 — and let his exposition send you back to Scripture rather than replace it.
  • Turn each chapter into prayer. Where Murray urges surrender, stop and actually pray the surrender. He would rather you gave up one thing to God than admired ten of his sentences.
  • Read the companion books. Pair the chapter on waiting with Murray’s Waiting on God, which unfolds the same theme over thirty-one short readings. The two together form a gentle school of the surrendered life.

Above all, resist the urge to treat this as information. Murray wrote to change how you live tomorrow morning, not to add a book to your shelf.

For reflection

Use these questions alone or in a group, after reading the chapters they draw on.

  1. Reading Paul’s description of the carnal Christian (1 Corinthians 3:1-3), where do you honestly recognize yourself — and what has kept you a “babe” rather than a spiritual believer?
  2. Murray says there are only two lives, the self-life and the Christ-life. Where in your daily life is the self-life still quietly in charge?
  3. What would it mean, concretely this week, to reckon yourself dead to sin and alive to God in Christ (Romans 6:11)?
  4. Murray calls waiting on God the beginning of prayer (Psalm 62:1). How might your prayer change if you began in silence rather than in speech?
  5. Is there one thing — a plan, a right, a grievance — that God is asking you to surrender so that Christ may be all in all in you?

Whenever you are ready, the whole book waits for you, free to read: begin with The Master’s Indwelling, and explore more of Andrew Murray when you are done.
